opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the cleanest way to see it is to count how many bits you actually get per example. With a hard label, say a one-hot class out of a thousand, the most you learn from one example is about log of a thousand, around ten bits. Usually it's less than that, because once the model is fairly confident the gradient from that label is mostly saying "yes, still cat." Soft targets hand you the teacher's whole distribution. Now the student isn't just told "this is a cat." It's told "this is mostly a cat, a bit like a lynx, slightly like a fox, and nothing like a truck." That's what Hinton called dark knowledge. The relative probabilities on the wrong answers carry the structure of the similarity space the teacher learned, and with a hard label you'd need a huge number of examples to recover that structure statistically.

A second way to put it is variance reduction. A hard label is a single noisy sample from something like the true conditional distribution. The teacher has already done the work of averaging over many examples and is giving you its estimate of the expectation directly. So you're regressing onto a smoothed, low-variance target instead of a stochastic one. Each gradient step points in a much more consistent direction, and you need fewer of them.

There's also a function-matching angle. When you match logits or a full distribution, you're constraining the student's function at that input along many dimensions at once, not just at the argmax. If you go further and match on augmented or off-distribution inputs, which the "knowledge distillation is a good teacher" work leaned on, you're basically probing the teacher's function wherever you like and copying it. That's far more supervision than the original dataset ever had.

In language models this gets even stronger. With next-token prediction on raw text, every position gives you one sampled token. With logit distillation you get the teacher's full distribution over the vocabulary at every position, so each sequence carries maybe orders of magnitude more information. And the teacher's distribution is learnable by construction. It came from a network, so it sits in the space of functions a network of that kind can represent. Raw data has irreducible noise and weird long-tail stuff the student would waste capacity chasing. The teacher has already denoised it and turned it into a curriculum the student can actually fit.

So my intuition is this: the teacher has compressed a huge amount of data into a function, and distillation lets the student read that function out directly, rather than rebuilding it from the same noisy samples the teacher had to struggle through.

r001.rationale: It contrasts a one-hot label’s limited information with the teacher’s full probability distribution, which supplies similarity information across classes per example.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the cleanest way to see it is in terms of how many bits of information each training example actually carries.

With a hard label, you're getting something like log of the vocabulary size worth of information, and really less than that, because most of the time the right answer is pretty predictable from context. You see "the cat sat on the" and the label is "mat," and the student already assigned a decent probability to "mat," so the gradient is small and you've learned very little. The label is one point sampled from a distribution, and a sample is a noisy, low-bandwidth channel to the thing you actually want, which is the distribution itself.

With soft targets, the teacher is handing you the entire distribution. So in the "cat sat on the" example, you don't just learn "mat," you learn that "couch" and "floor" and "rug" are also plausible, that "mat" is more likely than "rug," and that "the" and "quantum" are essentially zero. That's the dark knowledge idea from Hinton, and I think people underrate just how much structure is in those near-zero probabilities. The ratios between unlikely tokens encode an enormous amount of what the teacher knows about similarity, about syntax, about world knowledge. Every single token position becomes a dense supervision signal instead of a sparse one.

The other way I think about it is variance reduction. When you train on hard labels from the internet, the data is generated by some process, humans typing, and you're trying to infer the process from the samples. There's irreducible sampling noise in that. The teacher has already done the work of averaging over a huge number of samples, so what it emits is a much lower-variance estimate of the target. You're essentially training on a denoised version of the dataset. That's why you can get away with far fewer tokens: the student isn't paying the price of re-estimating all that noise.

There's also a nice optimization story. The soft target is a smooth function of the input, whereas hard labels are discontinuous. So the loss landscape the student sees is much better behaved, and the gradients at every position point in a consistent direction instead of jumping around based on which token happened to get sampled. Hinton's temperature trick is really just a way to turn up the contrast on those small probabilities so the student pays attention to them.

What I find interesting is that this suggests the bottleneck in pretraining isn't really compute, it's the information density of the supervision. We spend a huge amount of flops to extract a tiny signal from each hard token. Distillation is a demonstration that if you had a better oracle, you could learn the same thing with a fraction of the data. The catch, of course, is that you need the teacher first. The student can't exceed the teacher on the things the teacher is confidently wrong about, because the distribution it's imitating is wrong in exactly the same way. So I see distillation as a compression technique more than a way to get new capability, but as a compression technique it's remarkably efficient, and the per-sample efficiency falls directly out of the fact that you're learning from a distribution instead of a draw from it.

r001.rationale: The response says hard labels provide a noisy, low-bandwidth sample, while soft targets provide the full distribution and dense supervision at each position, yielding more information per example.

astra-6.text:
I think the intuition is that soft targets tell you much more than whether you got the answer right. They tell you something about the relationships between possible answers.

If I show you a picture of a dog and give you a hard label, all you learn is, “This is a dog.” But if the teacher assigns some probability to wolf and almost no probability to airplane, that gives you a much richer signal. You learn which mistakes are understandable and which ones are really far off. With a hard target, those alternatives are all just wrong.

So one example is carrying information that the teacher accumulated across many examples. The student doesn’t have to rediscover all of that structure from individual labels; it can inherit some of it through the teacher’s distribution.

I wouldn’t claim that’s a complete explanation, but that’s how I think about the sample efficiency: you’re getting a richer lesson from each example.

r001.rationale: The candidate explains that soft targets convey richer information about relationships among possible answers than hard labels, letting each example teach more and improving sample efficiency.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that a soft target tells you much more than whether you got the answer right. Suppose you’re classifying an image, and the label is “cat.” A hard target just says: put all the probability on cat. But the teacher might say it’s mostly a cat, with some probability of being a dog and almost no probability of being an airplane. That tells you something about the structure of the problem—which distinctions are ambiguous and which are obvious.

So each example gives you a much richer training signal. You’re learning some of the generalization that the teacher acquired from other examples, rather than having to reconstruct it from scratch.

Another way to think about it is variance reduction. A hard label is one observation. If the teacher’s distribution is a good approximation to the underlying conditional distribution, training against it gives you a less noisy estimate of what you should learn. Of course, you also inherit the teacher’s mistakes. But when the teacher is good, you can get much more information out of each sample.

r001.rationale: The response says soft targets provide a richer signal than hard labels, encoding ambiguity and class relationships so each example conveys more information.
